#8456. Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (685 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
  • Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai.
  • The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai.

The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition. That’s because the movement of ad budgets from linear to streaming has hardly been evenly paced.

Streaming’s share of ad revenue is indeed growing at major media companies, including The Walt Disney Company, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. But their earnings tell a different story: Linear revenue is falling faster than streaming revenue is rising. The shift is happening, but it’s not benefiting content owners as expected.

The core problem is a supply-demand imbalance. Streaming ad revenue is growing through increased volume, not higher prices. Newly introduced inventory floods in, making cheap inventory abundant. As major subscription services continue to promote free ad-supported streaming tiers, the buyers’ market will only continue.

Recent findings suggest that the solution is to grow demand, not increase prices. Fortunately, the ad dollars needed to support the streaming market already exist, sitting in local and midmarket budgets that haven’t been able to buy national CTV efficiently. The opportunity is to bring these advertisers into the broader video and streaming market, then develop ways to keep them investing.

Correcting the imbalance requires creating upcoming demand, then ensuring that content quality and product performance are strong enough to eventually shift pricing dynamics.

When it comes to growth, the glut of cheap national SVOD supply may be a problem for programmers, but it’s an opportunity for local and midmarket advertisers. If the current streaming market is largely aimed at Fortune 500 companies, the industry has to consider the thousands of smaller advertisers that make steady annual investments in local linear buys. Taken collectively, these advertisers represent billions of dollars in ad budgets.

Industry observers note that because these advertisers have smaller budgets, many haven’t tried streaming. It is more cost-efficient for them to execute local and spot buys on linear than to invest in targeted or national streaming campaigns. These advertisers are still seeing real success reaching millions of linear viewers, so they understand the power of TV. They just need an entry point for CTV. Solving this issue would allow demand to flow steadily into the market.

Once that demand enters the market, additional steps must happen. CPMs fall when inventory is sold as undifferentiated tonnage. With platforms like Disney+ and Netflix exploring free ad-supported tiers, even more low-cost supply will enter the market. But cheap supply that doesn’t perform isn’t worth an advertiser’s investment. If that inventory doesn’t deliver results for advertisers outside the Fortune 500, those advertisers will invest their budgets elsewhere, creating another demand imbalance.

Recent findings suggest that the answer lies in household addressability. While this is available on some streaming platforms, it’s still largely absent from the overall TV market, including linear. Household-level addressability turns cheap impressions into targeted impressions worth buying, even within highly premium inventory. The more information brands have about who will see their ads and whether those ads are likely to resonate with the viewer, the more they are likely to pay.

It is no secret that streaming is the future of TV, and shifting revenue numbers reflect that. To build a sustainable future for media companies and advertisers, the entire ecosystem must first provide ease of access and then addressability.

Making streaming easier to buy at scale would help solve the demand problem. Once more advertisers are in the market, addressability creates greater competition for impressions, solving the pricing imbalance.

This future is out there, provided the industry takes a few steps in the right direction.

Partner insights from Viamedia.ai.

Week of Nov 9 Evening News Ratings: WNT and CBS Evening News Grow

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Adweek

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A week after the midterm elections and the week the FAA issued a ground stop for all planes flying over the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that with more than 9 million total viewers for the second week in a row, WNT had its largest viewership since the week of Feb.
  • Recent findings suggest that note: The weekly averages of ABC News and NBC News are based on four days (Tuesday to Friday, and Monday to Thursday, respectively).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A week after the midterm elections and the week the FAA issued a ground stop for all planes flying over the U.S. airspace, ABC World News Tonight with David Muir and CBS Evening News with Tony Dokoupil finished with gains in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo for the week of Nov. 9.

Industry observers note that with more than 9 million total viewers for the second week in a row, WNT had its largest viewership since the week of Feb. 15, 2021. It continued to be the most-watched program on TV, including broadcast and cable (excluding sports).

Recent findings suggest that note: The weekly averages of ABC News and NBC News are based on four days (Tuesday to Friday, and Monday to Thursday, respectively). Monday’s broadcast (11/09/26) of ABC News was retitled to WNT, and Friday’s (11/13/26) edition of NBC Nightly News was retitled to NBC Nitely News. These broadcasts were excluded from the weekly and season averages.

According to Nielsen national live plus same-day Big Data + Panel and program ratings, ABC World News Tonight averaged 9.251 million total viewers and 1.366 million Adults 25-54 demo viewers for the week of Nov. 9. The evening newscast was up 1% in total viewers and 3% in the A25-54 demo compared to the previous week. Compared to the same week in 2025 (the week beginning Nov. 10), WNT was up 22%* in total viewers and 42% in the demo.

Industry observers note that NBC Nightly News with Tom Llamas finished as the No.2 newscast in total viewers and the demo, averaging 7.117 million and 1.161 million viewers, respectively. Compared to the previous week, Nightly News was down by 2% in total viewers and flat in the demo–the only broadcast not to see any growth in any of the measured categories. Compared to the same week a year ago, Nightly News was up by 7% in total viewers and 30% in the demo.

Finally, CBS Evening News finished the week of Nov. 9 with 4.633 million total viewers and 689,000 demo viewers. CBS News’ newscast saw an audience lift of 7% in total viewers and 4% in the demo compared to the previous week. Same-week, year-ago numbers showed CBS Evening News grew by 11% in total viewers and 31% in the demo.

*Note: ABC’s 2025 national availability was limited due to a carriage dispute between Disney and YouTube TV.

November 9, 2026 (Nielsen Substantial Data + Panel):.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are hiring 2026 and 2027 Graduate Software Engineers into engineering teams around the world.
  • It has been revealed that if you are excited about the potential that open source has for humanity and the enterprise, you have outstanding results in your academic career, and you are excited to contribute to the open source stack, this is the best way to apply to Canonical.
  • Sources indicate that most of our engineering teams work from home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are hiring 2026 and 2027 Graduate Software Engineers into engineering teams around the world. As a global platform organization we offer a wide range of software engineering challenges, in both open source products and commercial business systems. We have teams that work in a variety of languages, typically Python, Golang, Rust, C/C++, JavaScript and of course... Bash. We work from the very lowest levels of the Linux system - BIOS and boot loaders, firmware, kernel and drivers, all the way up to desktop applications and containers. We work on tiny devices like the Raspberry Pi and newly introduced RISC-V boards, all the way up to supercomputers, clouds and Kubernetes clusters. We work on compilers and toolchains, and we work on security, cryptography, performance and documentation. Some of our teams focus on packaging thousands of pieces of software, others focus on deep contributions to a single body of code.

It has been revealed that if you are excited about the potential that open source has for humanity and the enterprise, you have outstanding results in your academic career, and you are excited to contribute to the open source stack, this is the best way to apply to Canonical. We will work with you to identify teams and projects that would be interesting and a good fit for your skills and motivations. The process is highly competitive, it will require effort and excellence to succeed if you apply here.

Sources indicate that most of our engineering teams work from home. We try to align a single team in a single time zone - EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia Pacific and Indian Ocean), and AMER (North, South and Central Americas). Even though you work from home, we try to ensure you always have colleagues alongside to coach and mentor you, and for the companionship of shared problem solving and pair programming. Larger projects have multiple teams and might span the globe. We work with the open source community and specialize in building teams that work well in the 'fishbowl' of open source engineering. This is full time work, five days a week, often solving hard problems with significant responsibility. We don't generally work weekends and nights and we do enjoy good holidays but we also expect productive and intense engagement Monday to Friday.

According to recent reports, we bring all our engineering teams together in person twice a year for a deep 'sprint' with other teams to stimulate discussion and enable a wide range of career development paths. This is a fantastic way to demonstrate and develop your skill in software, learn about a wide range of technologies, make a meaningful impact to open source, and see some very interesting newly introduced cities that you might never otherwise get to visit.

If you find the open source stack amazing, and you have been a consistent high-performing student in your school and university, then this will be a challenging and exciting start to your career.

Location: This is a Globally remote role.

In a recent development, we consider geographical location, experience, and performance in shaping compensation worldwide. We assess performance and revisit compensation twice annually to ensure we recognize outstanding colleagues. In addition to base pay, we offer a performance-driven annual bonus or commission. We provide all team members with additional benefits which reflect our values and ideals. We balance our programs to meet local needs and ensure fairness globally.

Industry observers note that canonical is a pioneering tech firm at the forefront of the global move to open source. Our platform, Ubuntu, is very widely used in breakthrough enterprise initiatives such as public cloud, data science, AI, engineering innovation, and IoT. Our customers include the world's leading public cloud and silicon providers, and industry leaders in many sectors. We are founder-led, profitable, and growing.

Powered by worldwide distributed collaboration since our inception in 2004, we believe tech and business leadership can emerge anywhere. We have no central headquarters. Most of us work from home, but we are exceptionally disciplined about this. We have very high expectations of all colleagues, and are champions of excellence. Working here is a step into the future and will challenge you to think differently, work smarter, learn new skills, and raise your game.

Sources indicate that we are proud to foster a workplace free from discrimination. Diversity of experience, perspectives, and background create a better work environment and better products. Whatever your identity, we will give your application fair consideration.

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

OpenAI rewrites ChatGPT Business Hub terms after legal language raises concerns

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
  • OpenAI has revised the terms for its upcoming ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch.
  • Industry observers note that released last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

OpenAI has revised the terms for its upcoming ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch. The change came after Digiday reported that lawyers viewed the original language as potentially limiting businesses’ ability to bring certain legal claims against the tech giant.

Industry observers note that released last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics. For publishers, it’s a first-party view of activity they’ve largely had to estimate.

Before the revision, Section 10 of OpenAI’s terms of service for businesses using ChatGPT appeared to require those businesses to give up certain legal claims against OpenAI, lawyers told Digiday. They remarked the language could apply to claims involving content published on their websites, before they signed up.

Alan Chapell, privacy expert and founder of Chapell and Associates, remarked publishers who signed up for ChatGPT’s Business Hub and accepted the terms could have faced restrictions on how they pursued such claims against OpenAI.

The terms included a mandatory arbitration provision and class-action waiver, potentially requiring businesses to resolve disputes individually and outside of court, Chapell stated. The provision was broadly worded to cover certain claims that arose before the agreement was accepted, he explained.

Businesses had 30 days to opt out of arbitration, but if they did not, they could have faced limits on their ability to obtain evidence, pursue appeals and establish legal precedent through public court proceedings, Chapell added.

Hours after Digiday first contacted OpenAI on Nov. 18, the terms were revised. They now include a waiver of businesses’ rights to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data, according to an IP and tech lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

“There are still some restrictions here but they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse. A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages,” they mentioned.

Industry observers note that when approached for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the previous version of the terms “were not intended to cover this scenario,” and confirmed it updated the terms on Nov. 18.

“We continually evaluate the language in our Terms to make sure they are as clear as possible,” the spokesperson added in a statement. “The updated terms replace the separate ‘covered claims’ provision with language in Section 5.2 that ties the release to claims arising from a business’s Business Agent, including the use of customer data with that agent.”.

One industry exec, who requested anonymity, told Digiday they advised publishers’ legal teams to be cautious around some of the potential implications of OpenAI’s terms for businesses, after they were originally published on Nov. 10.

Although the terms have been revised, several lawyers who spoke to Digiday stated the original version was likely deliberate.

According to recent reports, “This is certainly not an oversight because they put these terms out there,” stated Gary Kibel, partner at law firm Davis+ Gilbert, which advises media and advertising clients. “It was incredibly intentional, and they were seeking to use this opportunity to get a release and wavier for any of these claims. It seems to be quite aggressive to do that.”.

Kibel said the revised terms still require businesses to waive certain legal claims related to their use of ChatGPT Business Hub and its AI Business Agents (essentially a business-specific chatbot), but no longer extend that waiver to unrelated legal disputes with OpenAI.

OpenAI’s changes come just weeks after Meta faced major backlash from publishers over its newly introduced commercial terms, which would have allowed the firm to scrape the websites of Meta Business account people. The proposed changes spurred a global, coordinated pushback from publishers, trade bodies, and government officials and regulators. In response, Meta confirmed it would pause the rollout until it has had time to explain the changes to key stakeholders and partners.

Industry observers note that openAI’s terms revision also follows tensions between publishers and AI companies over the use of published content. Documents unsealed in The Newly introduced York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft two months ago revealed tech giants were treating published content as free fuel for AI products that threatened their very existence.

Whatever prompted the revision, it may do little to ease publishers’ broader concerns about how AI companies use their content, and the terms attached to latest tools built around that content.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has its own content creator cottage industry, with millions of views and a crowded, competitive marketplace.

ChatGPT’s fresh AI visibility and click data can help inform publishers’ GEO strategies and complement third-party analytics.

Creators are tapping into their massive content libraries for syndication opportunities that pay dividends.

Why more brands are paying creators to make their ads

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, join us Dec.
  • Recent findings suggest that this article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most notable information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics.
  • According to recent reports, brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Recent findings suggest that this article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most notable information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics. More from the series →.

According to recent reports, brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy. Creative agencies might want to take note.

Recent findings suggest that “You get the authentic, scroll-stopping content that people want to engage each with. But you also get the reach,” said Katy Ball, head of social at M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment.

As spending on paid social channels — and video in particular — continues to rise, demand for creative assets to appear in those ad slots is increasing.

Recent findings suggest that the number of assets attached to individual campaigns has risen 30% in the last five years, according to a CreativeX study of 115,990 ad campaigns, representing $11 billion in ad spend. Per the study, just five assets receive 88% of media investment in an average campaign.

The need for more campaign assets is fueling the growth of asset-led spending, the fastest growing segment of the creator economy, according to a report published this week by research consultancy Madison & Wall.

Currently, 12% of the $112 billion spent on creators globally goes towards creators producing ads on behalf of brands, per the study. That’s expected to rise 16% every year through 2030.

According to recent reports, the days when brands principally paid creators to rent their following are rapidly disappearing. Influencers are now media partners, ambassadors and increasingly, cogs in the creative production supply chain. And brands see creator-made ads as a solution to their social asset shortage.

“For us, the appeal is simple. Buying space in someone’s feed doesn’t mean you’ve earned their attention. Good creators understand what their audiences care about and how to give them something worth stopping for,” said Jared Kozel, co-founder and chief creative officer at agency Super Nice. “That’s valuable creative judgment to bring into an ad no matter the brand or category.”.

Influencer marketing experts note that several different but related practices are included under the broader umbrella of creator-led production.

While some brands simply pay creators a fee in order to receive video or still assets for use in a campaign, whitelisting (also called “dark advertising”) has become a favored method of managing such arrangements.

In this context, an influencer grants a brand limited access to their social media accounts, allowing them to book a paid media campaign through that account, using assets made by the creator while taking advantage of discrete audience targeting.

“What we’re seeing is a lot of recutting of media spend to be allocated towards creator development in order to fund whitelisting,” mentioned Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social.

Madison & Wall’s research suggested that funding for creative production may also be coming from PR, social or experimental budgets, as well as traditional media or production pots of money.

Another related practice, user generated content, sees brands paying regular social media owners to license their content as creative assets in ad campaigns.

“They have to feed their their content engines, and they’re opening up as many different avenues as they can,” said Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo.

The relative low cost of working with influencers, versus creative production agencies, is the primary driver behind brand spending on creator-made assets.

According to recent reports, although production spending is often a small fraction of an overall campaign budget, marketers are keen to squeeze every non-working (that is, non-media) dollar for all it’s worth. While that same desire is pushing some brands toward generative AI production techniques, others are turning to creators.

It has been revealed that but as this type of spending grows, so to does the need to manage it effectively. “It’s never been more complicated to negotiate usage rights or exclusivity,” said Wedderburn.

Billion Dollar Boy, for example, recently added features to its Companion creator management tool designed to better facilitate creator-led production efforts and manage usage rights negotiations.

“The creator economy has never been more competitive, heightening the urgency for brands to understand the market context,” noted Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innocation officer and co-founder.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, increased brand spending in this area is already leading to an uptick in the fees commanded by some creators. Last year, agency practitioners reported creator rates ticking up 10-20% due to demand for expanded rights.

There’s also some evidence to show that creator-made assets perform as well as, or even better than, traditional advertising spots in a social context.

A report by System1, WPP Media and Goat published in June found that creator ads achieved 3.2X the brand-awareness lift for category leader ads as traditional advertising creative.

“We’re seeing a lot of brands say that is more valuable in terms of conversion and reach than some of the quick-and-dirty assets they previously would have relied on,” said Wedderburn.

In a recent development, that’s not unexpected. Audiences recognize the visual cues, language and production methods employed by creators as native to TikTok or Instagram, while clocking films shot on a closed set or using more traditional methods as foreign that same environment, a lesson that major advertisers like Nike are reluctantly absorbing.

Sources indicate that “If programs are set up correctly, creators can deliver volume and variety faster and more cost effectively than a traditional production cycle,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer, Viral Nation. “The shift we’re seeing is brands starting to proposal creators across their media budgets, rather than as a separate influencer line item alone.”.

Consulting giants Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

With shareholders, an $895 billion compute bill and a costly free tier, Anthropic’s no-ads pledge may have a shelf life.

Anthropic states no to ads but Wall Street may have other ideas

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
  • Anthropic is a public manufacturer now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.
  • Industry observers note that unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Anthropic is a public manufacturer now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.

Industry observers note that unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads. It went as far as spending Super Bowl money on a campaign mocking OpenAI for bringing them to ChatGPT. Its prospectus, the document pitching those public shares to investors, leaves advertisers out of the business altogether.

“Is it cynical to expect Anthropic to follow the same route? Not really. More like an educated guess,” said ad tech expert Shirley Marschall.

Besides, the company has already left the door open, she continued. Its pledge rules out sponsored links adjacent to conversations, but in the same post it indicates it will keep building features that help people “find, compare, or buy products, connect with businesses.” And once an agent recommends products, retail media will pay to be in those recommendations, Marschall mentioned, before adding: “Let’s see Anthropic turn that ad revenue down,” she added.

Recent findings suggest that advertisers, for their part, will be watching closely, and with mixed feelings. On the one hand, a latest media seller means a new platform to wrangle and one more set of tools and teams to learn at a time when most are still working out how to buy ChatGPT. On the other hand, Claude’s audience is also spending more and more time in those conversation threads. For marketers, that’s a hard place to stay out of for long.

“Anthropic, like any firm, has a stance towards handling consumer data and inadvertently how advertising is considered,” said independent ad tech consultant Jonathan D’Souza Rauto. “But monetization is a lucrative form of revenue. I’d expect Anthropic to have a change of heart. Look no further to how Apple has played this advertising game over the past few years despite being considered anti-advertising.”.

Life as a public company isn’t cheap, after all, and it’s even less cheap for an AI company that has signed up for approximately $895.4 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, some running to 2045. That’s more than 13 years of revenue at its current pace, given Q3 revenue of $17 billion. The revenue covering that bill is far less locked in since 80% of revenue is consumption-based and the S-1 notes many customers can cut usage or terminate on short notice. In fact, the company has already warned that “operating margins may compress when large tranches arrive.”.

Then there’s the free tier. “Free and promotional users may never convert to paid prepares,” the filing admits, yet Anthropic still pays to serve every one of them. Analysts found that cost sits in sales and marketing out of sight of the headline margin. That arrangement holds as long as free users keep upgrading. If they stop, Anthropic is left with a growing audience it pays to serve and earns nothing from.

In a recent development, openAI has already shown what that audience could be worth. ChatGPT ads reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launching. When both companies are trading, analysts will ask Anthropic why it’s leaving money on the table.

“They’ll go after advertising, just not in the way some assume,” said Rob Webster, founder and CEO of TAU Marketing Solutions. “The prize for Anthropic isn’t ads inside Claude. Advertising is now a trillion-dollar market, and the real power sits with whatever brain coordinates it: deciding what runs, where, and why. That’s a far more valuable position than selling impressions. Anthropic wants to be a new, better Microsoft or Apple. Selling tools to businesses. Not ad opportunities.”.

There are reasons, though, why Anthropic may resist the lure of ads for as long as it feasibly can.

Sources indicate that “Trust and impartiality really matter with LLMs, particularly among enterprise customers,” noted Alex Tait, founder of Entropy. “In contrast to OpenAI, Anthropic is at the moment approaching operating break-even without ads suggesting its existing business model could be commercially sustainable without it.”.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s anti-ads stance is based on its perspective that once ads become part of a business’s revenue targets, the pressure to maximize engagement can start influencing product decisions. For an AI app, in this case Claude, that creates a conflict: users expect Claude to help them make decisions in their own interests, not towards whatever generates revenue for the tech giant or its advertisers. And in its IPO prospectus, the company noted that they want “Claude’s only incentive to be giving them [users] a helpful answer,” which is why they have “chosen not to introduce that pressure [ads] into Claude.”.

Anthropic did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment.

Disney Advertising Hopes to Give Brands Multiple Layups This College Basketball Season

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An action-packed college basketball calendar is underway for Disney and its media sports properties, giving advertisers and brands access to a passionate, loyal audience ready to follow their teams all the way to the men’s and women’s tournaments in March.
  • For the first time, Disney’s college basketball offering this season includes exclusive coverage of the Players Era Tournament, as well as exclusive coverage of ACC and SEC games, two of the sport’s most competitive conferences.
  • In addition, the conglomerate will also air the State Farm Champions Classic, ACC/SEC Challenge, Champ Week, NCAA Women’s Tournament, and Jimmy V Classic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An action-packed college basketball calendar is underway for Disney and its media sports properties, giving advertisers and brands access to a passionate, loyal audience ready to follow their teams all the way to the men’s and women’s tournaments in March.

For the first time, Disney’s college basketball offering this season includes exclusive coverage of the Players Era Tournament, as well as exclusive coverage of ACC and SEC games, two of the sport’s most competitive conferences.

In addition, the conglomerate will also air the State Farm Champions Classic, ACC/SEC Challenge, Champ Week, NCAA Women’s Tournament, and Jimmy V Classic.

All in all, more than 6,000 men’s and women’s basketball games during the regular season will air across ESPN, ESPN+, ACC Network, SEC Network, and SEC Network+.

“College sports fans choose their team once and stay for life, which makes them really rare for audiences and brands,” noted Jacqueline Dobies, vp, revenue and yield management at Disney Advertising, to ADWEEK.

The Disney executive noted that they connect with fans differently, saying they don’t make fans come to them; instead, through its various rights, it reaches fans across linear, streaming, digital, and social, giving advertisers and brands multiple options to access this ravid fan base.

Dobies pointed out that its data stack enables Disney Advertising to ensure each access option works for the brands it serves.

“You know, a brand can reach everything from like a prime broadcast fan to a weeknight streaming fan to a fan that’s viewing the highlights on mobile or social,” she noted, adding, “and we can consistently measure across all of those things.”.

More than half of 200 advertisers from last year are back for another season, and they are growing their investment in Disney’s college basketball programming across the portfolio, according to Dobies. Disney has added more than 20 new advertisers and two new product categories this year – exercise equipment and athletic wear.

According to recent reports, this extensive advertiser inventory comes as ESPN comes off its most-watched men’s college basketball regular season in 11 years, with viewership up 25% year over year. On the women’s side, ESPN had its most-watched regular season since 2008-09, with viewership up 19% from the year prior.

Dobies disclosed that the media manufacturer does not publicly share how much ad income Disney generated from its college basketball programming, but mentioned this year they are “pacing double digits ahead when we look at men’s and women’s combined.” She added that income from both men’s and women’s college basketball is growing.

Disney Advertising is also seeing strong demand for college basketball in its longer upfront marketplace. Dobies says that as teams and matchups become more competitive and individual games become sought out, they will see an increase in the scatter marketplace for those really competitive matchups that couldn’t be predicted at the beginning of the season.

Even surrounding college basketball programs are being sought after by brands and advertisers.

College GameDay, for example, has additionally seen growth in sponsorships, with seven brands activating across men’s and women’s programming, three of which are upcoming to College GameDay.

Dobies says College GameDay “is definitely a very sought-after space for advertisers” because they can also activate on-site, and viewers can see that, providing additional reach.

Disney Advertising has also secured more than 20 sponsors across the season, seven of which are new. They have also sold additional title and presenting sponsorships across more than 40 multi-team non-conference events this fall.

With audiences growing, returning advertisers increasing their investment, and a packed slate of marquee matchups, standout players, and top teams giving brands even more reasons to lean in, Disney is hoping for multiple slam dunks this college basketball season.

“Because we have such a robust college basketball schedule, when you invest with Disney college basketball, you’re more likely to be a part of those lightning-in-a-bottle moments, those upsets, the rushing of the court. Those are the things that you can’t predict, that you only see in college sports,” stated Dobies.

#8436. Breaking: Future of Marketing Briefing: Consulting firms revive their marketing ambitions in the C-suite the holdcos covet

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2602 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: Future of Marketing Briefing: Consulting firms revive their marketing ambitions in the C-suite the holdcos covet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
  • This Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m.
  • However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

This Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

Sources indicate that deloitte Digital’s offer is Converge, an operating system that strings together AI agents to run marketing and sales work, from research and briefs through to campaign deployment and deal tracking. Some of the agents are Deloitte’s own. Others are ones a client already runs elsewhere, and the whole thing plugs into the tools and clout contracts a brand is already paying for. Marketing and sales versions are live, with commerce on the way, and Deloitte pitches them as one front-office system tied to revenue, which it calls “brand to cash.” Because it’s sold as a license that stretches across sales, marketing and service, it needs sign-off well above the CMO, which suits a consulting firm that’s used to having those conversations.

Recent findings suggest that accenture Song’s play in media, a market it has circled in the U.S. for years without committing. In September, it moved Melissa Fein, who built its media planning and buying business in Australia and New Zealand after leaving Initiative in 2024, to New York as U.S. media lead. This month it posted a job for a head of media strategy for the Americas. The ad describes a “new world media practice” with no legacy systems to protect, and asks for an AI-first strategist” to lead planning, build new tools and become the person senior clients call before a brief exists.

Candidates need hands-on command of econometrics, incrementality testing and attribution plus experience in significant-spending categories like financial services, telecommunications, automotive and health. Those are the categories where the ANZ team won Australia Post and Mediabank. Accenture Song Ndidi Oteh has kept quiet on specifics, saying only that whatever it does in media won’t take traditional forms.

“The real prize is the conversation before the brief,” said  Steve Boehler, founder of agency consultancy the Mercer Island Group. ”If you help define the business problem, design the operating model and decide how success will be measured, you are competing long before an agency review begins.”.

Both plays echo what the holdcos have spent 18 months engineering: operating systems that run a client’s marketing for it and media businesses that sell more than buying. The consultants may have the better shot at making either one stick. They already sit with the CEOs, CIOs and CFOs who sign off on systems spanning sales, marketing and service and installing that kind of software is their day job. A holdco operating system, rightly or wrongly, still reads as an agency tool, built partly to make the agency cheaper to run. Accenture also arrives in the U.S. media with no legacy buying business to protect, so it can lead with measurement and tools before it has to sell buying power.

Whether any of this translates is another matter. Consultancies have been trying to crack advertising for the best part of a decade, after all, and the media buying business still rewards a scale Accenture doesn’t yet have in the U.S. Then again, now is arguably as good a time as any for them to try, if not better. With Omnicom and IPG combined, big advertisers are down to three holdcos, and some are skipping the pitch one so a credible alternative has rarely been more useful. AI is also pushing decisions about how marketing works into rooms where the CFO and CIO sit, which consultancies have been in for years. And a C-suite that takes a closer look at marketing will start asking how agencies make their money, from data fees to principal media, which is an awkward question for any firm with a buying business to defend.

According to recent reports, “The consultancies may have an advantage in getting invited to design the system,” stated Boehler. “That is not the same as proving they can run marketing better. The client still needs evidence of better decisions, better work and better business outcomes, not just fewer handoffs.”.

Industry observers note that all of which makes the Publicis-WPP episode look a little quaint, partly because it was never quite the fight it was billed as. Sadoun spent months telling investors that Publicis was winning major accounts without a pitch. Rose, asked about it by an analyst, called it “this pitchless CEO handshake thing that I keep getting asked about” and said decisions that big deserve careful consideration. Publicis answered with an open letter treating that line as her theory, and the coverage did the rest. Somewhere along the way, a question about how clients choose agencies turned into a row about manners.

Industry observers note that what got lost was the shift both CEOs were describing. Significant advertisers are increasingly buying data, identity and AI infrastructure, which a six-week parade of slide decks was never built to judge, so some now test one partner in depth instead of auditioning several. Those decisions are also moving up the organization chart, to executives who sign off on systems not campaigns. That’s how consultancies have always been bought. Deloitte and Accenture are built for long, technical evaluations run by CFOs and CIOs, and while the holdcos; remarks were being turned into a grudge march one released a system that needs the c-suite’s signature and the other started building a U.S. media practice designed to win it.

Sources indicate that “Client CEOs and CMOs pay attention to CEOs of holdcos, especially when a transition in agency leadership occurs and the agency CEO conducts outreach to key clients,” said Gartner analyst Jay Wilson. “But most recognize that while agency CEOs may set a direction for the agency, that direction may be slow to take hold – or never take hold – within the agency teams doing the actual day-to- day work. A strong relationship with, or aversion to, an agency chief executive is usually more consequential at smaller, independent agencies.”.

Whatever gets agreed in the c-suite, someone still has to do the work.

Sources indicate that “The consultants don’t have to copy the incumbent model to compete,” remarked Boehler. “But they still have to do the work: initiative, negotiate, deliver, reconcile and prove results. A different model is a proposition until clients experience the difference.”.

Cinema admissions have climbed back on the strength of a fuller blockbuster slate and much of the ad money that shifted to digital during lockdowns stayed put. Most screens still sell their preshow through sales houses that have always sold offline.

Industry observers note that mikkel Hagedorn, a WPP and Omnicom alum, has spent five or six years building a platform that lets buyers book cinema spots programmatically, target them against specific films and count impressions straight off ticket sales. The firm is live in Denmark and Finland, where sales houses have handed it two minutes of a 15-minute preshow at a base CPM of around €75. Hagedorn’s bet is that exhibitors can bring cinema into the digital ad market while keeping the premium pricing newspapers gave away when they went programmatic.

His manufacturer, called Cinemataztic, gives buyers two ways to purchase inventory: first, agencies already running programmatic campaigns can reach the inventory through supply-side platforms and demand-side platforms such as Smartclip Google’s DV360 respectively, which lets cinema sit inside budgets that were going to be spread across other channels anyway, Advertisers who would rather skip the intermediary fees can book directly through Hagedorn’s own interface.

Either way, the buyer can pick what individual film they want to target, so a brand could run only against the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie if it likes. The impressions they buy come straight from exhibitors’ ticketing systems, which means one ticket sold counts as one impression. There are “no multipliers here,” remarked Hagedorn, a dig at the audience multipliers that inflate numbers elsewhere in media.

It has been revealed that so far a lot of the money has come from digital agencies edging up the funnel into brand work. Hagedorn mentioned he has seen little cannibalisation of advertisers still buying cinema the old way. He said the business has grown 50% a year and forecasts the same for next year, when the manufacturer expands into Sweden, Thailand and a third, bigger market he wouldn’t share.

In a recent development, even so, the programmatication of cinema will be a slow burn. Advertising is still its third-largest revenue line after tickets and concessions. Most hand it entirely to sales houses on contracts of three to five years and only learn that demand is falling when the next guarantee shrinks. Hagedorn has been warning them about this for years. “They cannot stay offline forever,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that brands that gatecrash cultural moments tend to stick to tournaments and royal weddings, and they rarely pick a game that lets players mug strangers in a fake Florida. Grand Theft Auto, the culture-warping franchise, is the exception, and its sixth installment is drawing the kind of guerilla marketing normally reserved for FIFA and the Olympics.

Anyone trying to keep up can follow the running tally at GTA6Brands.com, an independent tracker run by Mike Litman that logs a newly introduced stunt each day for his GTA 6 Marketing News podcast. Hardly anything in culture still sets off that kind of scramble across so many brands at once, and with GTA the explanation is scale.

In a recent development, “I’ve tracked over 290 brand moves around GTA 6 so far, including around 130 unofficial activations,” said Litman. “That’s a remarkable amount of marketing activity orbiting a product launch, particularly when so many of those brands have no formal relationship with Rockstar. What’s interesting is the range of brands getting involved.”.

Industry observers note that with media this fragmented, marketers have a shortlist of moments when a mass audience shows up at the same time, and most of those moments involve a ball. GTA earned its spot on that list over 13 years. When GTA 5 debuted in 2013 it made $1 billion in three days, which owner Take Two called a rate faster than any other video game, film or other entertainment product has ever managed. For context, Marvel’s “The Avengers” movie took 19 days to reach that number. In the years since it launched, the game has since surpassed 230 million units sold worldwide across three console generations. The wait for the sequel turned into an event of its own. GTA 6’s second trailer received 475 million views across all platforms within 24 hours of its release, beating the 365 million in 24 hours for Marvel’s Deadpool & Wolverine film. Take Two has issued $8 billion for its 2027 guidance for the fiscal year the game launches in. For a brand that wants a crowd all watching the same thing at once, that’s about as close to a World Cup final as entertainment gets, and nobody has to get past FIFA’s lawyers.

“I think the fascinating thing is that GTA 6 has achieved something usually reserved for the World Cup or Super Bowl, but without the stadium, the broadcast rights or the traditional sponsorship machinery,” mentioned Litman. “It’s become a cultural event in its own right. And brands aren’t waiting for permission to participate.”.

A few did get permission, though. Rockstar’s list of official partners is short and made up mostly of platforms. Sony signed an exclusive marketing deal, which put a “Plays Best on PS5” tag on the game’s official channels. Netflix got the “Extended Look” trailer six trailers before YouTube in August, in what Take Two boss Strauss Zelnick called a “groundbreaking partnership”. YouTube is running a 24-hour launch live livestream from its own channel, and the Miami Heat have redesigned court, custom uniforms and Vice City merchandise.

“Nike is going back to its roots and what built the brand: cultural relevance through people who have the trust of a community. It is a bold choice when most advertising pitches are about AI. Nike uses AI too, as a tool, but clearly highlights it understands that what stays scarce is trust. Trust comes from identity and proximity: who is speaking, and how close they are to the community listening. It also shows what creators and athletes must build to ask a brand like Nike for more than just a campaign fee. Most of them are offering access to an audience that belongs to a social or tech platform, targeted and measured with the data that the platform makes available. Global stars aside, only those who directly own the relationship with their audience and their data can negotiate a share of the long-term value.”.

— Alessandro De Zanche, founder of media consultancy ADZ Strategies on Nike’s bet on creators to drive growth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
  • We’re looking for a senior product designer to be the first dedicated designer on our product growth team, shaping how creators get set up, see value in their first days, and enjoy a seamless upgrade experience.
  • Product growth is a new team at Kit, formed earlier this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

We’re looking for a senior product designer to be the first dedicated designer on our product growth team, shaping how creators get set up, see value in their first days, and enjoy a seamless upgrade experience. Kit ships fast, and the product growth team builds the frameworks and systems that connect creators to the value in their initiative as the product keeps changing. We need a designer who can balance rapid experimentation with long-term value for our creators.

Product growth is a new team at Kit, formed earlier this year. In the six months since, we’ve found our rhythm and started to move the numbers, but we’re still shaping how we work, how we prioritise and where we focus in the long term. As the team’s designer, you’ll be the design voice for growth, with real influence over how the team works and what it builds.

It has been revealed that you'll own the design of the moments that move our funnel: onboarding, activation, free trials, upgrade and upsell flows, pricing and checkout, and billing. You'll work in a team that learns by shipping, through A/B tests and ship-and-measure changes, and you'll use data to decide what to try next.

This is a full-time IC role for a designer who loves connecting design decisions to numbers, moves swiftly without sacrificing quality, and is excited about using AI to accelerate outcomes.

We need someone who thinks deeply about user behaviour, interaction design and the product experience, and who is proactive about finding the next opportunity rather than waiting for a spec.

According to recent reports, you'll report to Dan Winer, Director of Product Design, and join a small, high-impact product design team right now consisting of four senior product designers and a senior design engineer. From day one, you’ll be part of the product growth team’s product trio alongside the product manager and engineering manager, shaping the team’s vision, priorities and how we work. You’ll also work closely with the team’s engineers.

It has been revealed that first week: Get to know Kit’s product and the product growth team’s goals. Get access to Figma, Linear, Mixpanel and our other reporting tools. Take part in get-to-know-you calls with the team.

Industry observers note that first month: Get up to speed on how we track and measure creator behaviour in Mixpanel, Omni and Clarity, which experiments are running now, and what we’ve learnt from past ones. Join the product trio’s planning and prioritisation discussions, and ship a small experiment or two, with support from the Director of Product Design as you take ownership of the growth work.

Recent findings suggest that first six months: Own design across the team’s work, which spans growth (onboarding, activation, trials and upgrades) and billing (checkout, plan changes, downgrades and cancellation). This might include personalising onboarding, improving free-to-paid conversion or simplifying our payment flows. By six months, the team should rely on you for a clear picture of how creators move through these flows, where they get stuck and why. You’ll help the team run more and better experiments, from forming a hypothesis to reading the results. We don’t have dedicated researchers, so you’ll talk to creators, run usability tests, track the impact of your work and proactively suggest iterations.

First year: Help the team improve our activation, free-to-paid, trial conversion, and early retention rates, so that more creators upgrade, stay on Kit, and find real value. Turn our upsell, discount and blueprint change moments into one coherent experience instead of a set of one-off prompts.

Interaction design for complex web applications, with a strong eye for visual hierarchy and detail.

Grounding design decisions in the creator’s voice through interviews, usability testing and customer feedback, partnering with the PM so it shapes what we build as well as how.

Designing flows that change depending on who’s seeing them, like free, trial and paid accounts, or creators upgrading and downgrading.

Designing onboarding, activation, upgrade, pricing, checkout or billing flows.

Experiment design and reading results, including knowing when an A/B test is the right approach or when to just ship and track.

Defining what events to track so the team can measure what you shipped, using tools like Mixpanel.

Clear written and visual communication of design rationale, including async walkthroughs.

Around 5+ years as a product designer on SaaS or other complex web-based products.

Led design on growth, monetisation or onboarding work and can point to its impact on metrics, ideally including retention or quality of conversion, not just volume.

Worked in a cross-functional team with a product manager and engineers, shipping continuously.

Worked within and contributed to an established design system.

A portfolio that highlights how research or data informed your decisions and what happened as a result.

Bonus: designed pricing, billing or plan change experiences.

Curious about why customers behave the way they do, and about what the numbers aren’t telling you.

Comfortable being wrong in public and sharing what you don’t know, not just what you do.

Proactive and self-directed, with a bias for shipping.

Excited about AI and pragmatic about how to use it.

Low ego and comfortable giving and receiving direct feedback.

Preferring to execute designs handed down from a product manager.

Treating a conversion win as the finish line, without checking whether those creators stay with Kit and find value.

Wanting long, highly-refined projects with little contact with data or results.

Discomfort with experiments that fail or with changing direction based on what we learn.

Focusing on visual polish without deeper thinking about user behaviour and business outcomes.

Being philosophically opposed to using AI in your work.

Needing well-established processes and a fully defined roadmap from day one.

We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at level 4 ($172,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

Industry observers note that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.     As an AI Forward Deployed ProcessOS is a new kind of Camunda product: business processes described in natural language, generated as executable BPMN workflows, and improved autonomously from production data. We’re hiring the first cohort of Forward Deployed Engineers to bring it into production at enterprise customers. You’ll own the deployment journey from first process file to a working, improving system, and hand off a functioning capability to the customer’s team. The code you write and the patterns you discover feed directly back into how ProcessOS is built. This is a rare opportunity to shape a product, a function, and a field practice from day one.

    You’ll work end‑to‑end across Java services and React interfaces, collaborating closely with a talented global team to measure, improve, and scale performance and fault tolerance in real-world distributed systems.

    It has been revealed that work at depth technically. Configure and run Camunda clusters locally and in cloud environments. Debug integration failures. Build custom agents where platform defaults don’t fit. Write connector logic that gets legacy enterprise systems talking to ProcessOS.

    Build the playbook. There is no deployment template yet. Document what good looks like as you discover it, and make the next implementation faster.

    In a recent development, feed the product. Custom integrations you write get contributed back. Integration patterns get codified. Production bugs you find, you often fix. Your field work is a direct input to ProcessOS.

    Hand off deliberately. Leave customers with a team that can operate independently, is trained on the platform, and acts on improvement results without you.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of November 9, 2026.

    As expected, the three cable networks could not maintain their midterm election-week momentum, declining in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

    Viewer interest remained high during the just-concluded week, driven by the breaking news of the FAA issuing a nationwide airplane groundstop on Friday, Nov. 13. Fox News was the most-watched network in total viewers on that day, while CNN finished on top in the prized demo.

    Interestingly, the FAA breaking news kept CNN in first place in the primetime demo for the second week in a row.

    According to Nielsen Significant Data + Panel, for the week of Nov. 9, Fox News averaged 1.584 million total viewers and 109,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network saw losses of 15% in total viewers and 33% in the demo compared with the prior week (the week beginning Nov. 2).

    Sources indicate that during total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.018 million total viewers and 93,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on the previous week’s average, the network was down by 9% in total viewers and 25% in the demo.

    Fox News remained second in total primetime viewership and slipped from third to fourth in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it remained first in total viewers and was in third place in the total day demo.

    According to recent reports, MS NOW averaged 1.077 million total viewers and 109,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network dropped by 30% in total viewers and 52% in the demo compared with its prior-week primetime average.

    Recent findings suggest that during total day, MS NOW averaged 674,000 total viewers and 73,000 demo viewers. It was down 27% in total viewers and 42% in the demo compared with the network’s average the prior week.

    Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW continued to be in third in total primetime viewers and fell from fourth to ninth in the demo. It ranked third in total viewers and was sixth in the total day demo.

    CNN averaged 802,000 total primetime viewers and 160,000 demo viewers. It saw declines of 40% in total viewers and 57% in the demo compared to the previous week.

    During total day, the network had 530,000 total viewers and 85,000 demo viewers. For CNN, total viewers were down 29%, and demo viewers were down 49% during this daypart.

    Among all cable networks, CNN remained in fourth place in total viewers and was the No. 3 network in the demo during primetime. It continued to be in fourth in total day among total viewers and was in the same position in the demo.

    Compared to their performance during the same period a year ago:.

    Fox News held 9 of the 15 spots among the week’s most-watched cable news reveals, with The Five in first place with 2.562 million total viewers at 5 p.m. ET. MS NOW’s top show was the 9 p.m. ET Monday airing of The Rachel Maddow Show in fourth place with 1.904 million total viewers. MS NOW had a total of six programs in the top 15 for the just-concluded week.

    The 15 top spots in the Adults 25-54 demo were populated with shows from all three cable networks. CNN’s Anderson Cooper 360, airing weeknights at 8 p.m. ET, was in first place with 229,000 demo viewers. CNN had a total of five shows in the top 15. Fox News’ Jesse Watters Primetime, airing weeknights at 8 p.m. ET, finished second with 223,000 demo viewers. Fox News had seven shows on the chart. Finally, MS NOW’s The Rachel Maddow Show was the network’s top show, with 166,000 demo viewers, ranking 12th. MS NOW had four shows in the chart.

    Week of November 9, 2026 (Nielsen Massive Data + Panel):.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • We are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch.
    • Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. We’ve built all of our technology in-house including an EHR, patient care admin system, patient portal, website, marketing technology etc. Winona has two compounding pharmacies and a team of in-house physicians providing world-class care via a fully vertically integrated business model.

    We are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch. This role spans campaign configuration and tracking, content and design review, and cross-platform QA — identifying and resolving complications before they reach our audience.

    Seniority Level: Junior–Mid Level.

    Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.

    Verify campaign and journey names against Winona’s naming conventions (name, year, event, medium and audience).

    Review journey configuration, including start tiles, suppressions, scheduled send dates and times, tile logic and conditionals, entry limits, exit rules and journey event tracking.

    Confirm that monthly and recurring journeys are refreshed with updated start tiles prior to each send.

    Verify that campaign labels are applied correctly (audience, segments, category, goal and month/year).

    Confirm that the appropriate conversion events are assigned for each campaign type: prospect, customer upsell, Shop, community and live event campaigns.

    Review delivery settings, including quiet hours, send time optimization, frequency caps and performance alerts.

    Verify that link tracking is configured correctly, including Google Analytics, UTM parameters and custom link parameters.

    Review sender details: message type, from name, from email and reply-to address.

    Review email templates against Winona’s brand and design standards, including fonts, sizing, padding, CTA button styling, link formatting and footers.

    Test all links, CTA buttons and image links, and confirm that images include alt text.

    Proofread copy for accuracy, consistency and formatting.

    Send and review test proofs in light and dark mode on iOS and Android, across both Gmail and Apple Mail.

    Coordinate SMS test sends with the appropriate team members prior to testing.

    Conduct QA on email touchpoints that connect to Shopify, such as Shop campaigns and checkout-related flows, to ensure a seamless end-to-end experience.

    Follow and help maintain internal templating documentation, QA checklists and the HTML template library.

    Communicate issues, errors and inconsistencies to the lifecycle team clearly and promptly, and track them through resolution.

    Recommend improvements to QA processes and standards on an ongoing basis.

    At least 3 years of experience performing QA within an ESP like Iterable or similar platforms.

    Working knowledge of HTML and CSS for email.

    Exceptional attention to detail and consistent checklist execution.

    Understanding of how emails render across clients, devices and dark mode.

    Clear written communication for reporting issues.

    Proficiency with Handlebars or dynamic content personalization.

    Shopify experience, particularly with checkout and order flows.

    Experience with email testing tools such as Litmus or Email on Acid.

    Familiarity with Google Analytics and UTM tracking.

    Experience with ClickUp or similar project management tools.

    Knowledge of SMS best practices and compliance standards (CAN-SPAM, CASL).

    As a full-time independent contractor, you’ll enjoy:.

    Remote-first, work wherever you choose.

    Paid non-working holidays per country of residence.

    Pro-rated 13th-month bonus in select regions.

    Financial support for online courses.

    Fun and casual work environment.

    Employee engagement activities and virtual gatherings.

    We are a diverse, global team! 🌍.

    Lead AI for CS: run intake and prioritization of use cases, manage rollout of Claude skills, agents and Camunda on Camunda automations, track consumption, cost, adoption and time saved, and own the communications and enablement behind each rollout.

    Act as the single front door for CS Operations and GTM Systems requests in these domains, turning ad-hoc asks into problem statements with goals and success criteria.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Experience owning customer health scoring, churn and expansion signals in B2B SaaS or enterprise software, ideally from CS Operations, CS Strategy or Revenue Operations.

    Experience validating data and testing whether a signal predicts outcomes using SQL or BI tools.

    A track record of driving cross-functional decisions with Product, Legal, Finance and CS leadership without direct authority.

    Clear writing: decision memos, playbooks and enablement content.

    Experience leading the business-side implementation of an enterprise system (requirements, UAT, rollout, change management) alongside a technical owner.

    Ability and/or willingness to use our product.

    Software licensing, entitlement management or usage-based pricing experience.

    Exposure to product telemetry and data privacy constraints (GDPR, consent-based data collection).

    Experience with self-managed or on-premises software where vendor visibility is limited.

    Hands-on experience running AI or automation programs, including using tools like Claude to build analyses, prototypes or agent workflows.

    Nice to have: familiarity with process orchestration or Camunda's customer base.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that supabase runs millions of Postgres databases, and storage performance is now one of the biggest levers on how fast, reliable, and affordable they are.
    • As the senior engineer driving storage, you'll own this effort end to end: the architecture and build-vs-buy decisions, integration into our compute platform, and operating the system in production.
    • Recent findings suggest that your first goal is raw Postgres I/O performance at scale.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that supabase runs millions of Postgres databases, and storage performance is now one of the biggest levers on how fast, reliable, and affordable they are. We're building a software-defined, NVMe-over-Fabrics storage platform underneath Supabase Postgres. Postgres stays unmodified, and the upcoming layer delivers near-local-NVMe performance with the durability and flexibility of networked storage.

    As the senior engineer driving storage, you'll own this effort end to end: the architecture and build-vs-buy decisions, integration into our compute platform, and operating the system in production.

    Recent findings suggest that your first goal is raw Postgres I/O performance at scale. In the longer term, the layer you build will provide the block-level snapshots and copy-on-write clones behind database branching, fast restores, and instant resizes. Because it's software-defined, it will also travel with us as we expand beyond a single cloud provider into multi-cloud and colocated infrastructure.

    This is a foundational, high-ownership role. You'll set the technical direction for storage at Supabase and help grow the team around it.

    Lead the architecture of Supabase's NVMe-oF storage platform, including evaluating and deciding between adopting existing software-defined storage and building on SPDK.

    Integrate networked block storage into our Kubernetes-based compute platform through CSI drivers and custom controllers, covering provisioning, attach/detach, resizing, and migration.

    Make Postgres fast on networked storage by profiling and tuning the full I/O path, from fsync, WAL, and checkpoints through the kernel block layer, NVMe/TCP, and the network.

    Design for durability and availability, including replication or erasure coding, failure domains, failover, and data-integrity verification.

    Build I/O isolation and QoS so that noisy neighbors can't degrade other tenants.

    Set performance and reliability SLOs, and build the benchmarking and observability to hold the system to them.

    Design the layer for block-level snapshots and copy-on-write clones, laying the groundwork for database branching.

    Keep the platform portable across AWS, other clouds, and bare-metal/colo.

    Write design docs, mentor engineers, and work closely with the Compute, Branching, Postgres, and Multicloud teams.

    Participate in on-call rotations, incident response, and post-incident reviews.

    Resolve escalated support problems, while also identifying and resolving systemic issues across the platform.

    Have 7+ years of software engineering experience, including significant time building and operating storage systems in production.

    Have built or operated distributed or software-defined block storage (for example Ceph RBD, Lightbits, Simplyblock, Portworx, LINSTOR/DRBD, or an in-house system).

    Have hands-on experience with NVMe/TCP or NVMe-oF, including targets, initiators, multipath, and failover behavior.

    Have a deep understanding of Linux storage internals: the block layer, io_uring, page cache, O_DIRECT and fsync semantics, filesystems, and device-mapper.

    Write strong systems code in Go, plus C, C++, or Rust.

    Measure performance rigorously with fio, pgbench, eBPF, and perf, and can explain latency down to its individual components.

    Understand durability tradeoffs between replication, erasure coding, and consistency under failure.

    Have led technical direction on a complex system: design docs, tradeoffs, and bringing others along.

    Have experience with Kubernetes controllers and/or CSI drivers.

    Have been on call for large production systems.

    Communicate clearly in writing and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Experience implementing block-level snapshots, thin provisioning, or copy-on-write cloning.

    Postgres internals knowledge (WAL, buffer manager, checkpointer), or familiarity with OrioleDB.

    Experience with AWS networking and instance storage at scale (ENA, placement, bandwidth limits).

    Experience running storage on bare metal or in colo.

    Contributions to open source storage projects or the Linux kernel storage stack.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    According to recent reports, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    It has been revealed that once a year, the entire company gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Industry observers note that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).
